newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA PRESIDENT URGES MINERS TO BACK REFORM.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA PRESIDENT URGES MINERS TO BACK REFORM.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu on Saturday told cheering coal miners who had demanded his resignation two months ago that they had no choice but to back reforms to restructure their inefficient industry.

Constantinescu visited Lupeni, 350 km (210 miles) west of Bucharest, on the 20th anniversary of a rare strike by miners who took high-ranking Communist Party officials hostage to press demands for better pay and conditions.

"I came here to tell you that you are not alone, you are not ignored and that you will not be forgotten," Constantinescu told 3,000 miners in a cold rain outside a colliery in the town, long a hotbed of trade union militancy in the Jiu Valley.
"We cannot go on with lies and with an economy which cannot produce and needs subsidies. We must carry out reforms. We must put an end to single-industry zones. They are finished."
"Emil, Emil!," cheered the crowd. Many miners jostled to get closer to the rostrum to shake the president's hand.

Twenty years after the revolt, life remains hard in the coalfield, where prospects for secure jobs are dwindling as the government proceeds with plans to close loss-making mines. Miners earn nearly twice the average monthly wage, equivalent to $80, but conditions are poor and equipment outdated.
In June, some 40,000 miners went on a two-week strike demanding the resignation of Constantinescu and his government. The government met some, but not all, of their pay demands.

The reformist Constantinescu, who defeated an ex-communist in last year's election, urged his government this week to move forward with reforms to meet International Monetary Fund demands. Ministers have been locked in sometimes bitter talks on revising the budget, a main IMF condition for fresh credits.
Constantinescu told the miners the government was discussing how to restructure industry with the IMF, including payouts for miners made redundant.

Vasile Caila, a leader of the 1977 revolt, said he had vivid memories of the confrontation between miners and communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, who bowed to their demand to come to the coalfield and hear their grievances.
"When he came, Ceausescu was black with rage but also very frightened," Caila told Reuters. "They were extraordinary days. We were ready to die, but we wanted our voices heard."

He said miners denounced Ceausescu, his sleeves rolled up worker-style, as a "pig" and "criminal" as he walked through the crowd. The communist leader met many of the miners' demands and returned to Bucharest but 14 unionists were later jailed.
Lupeni was also the focal point of a miners' strike in 1929, put down by authorities with troops. Historical accounts say 30 people died and 100 were wounded.

Like Ceausescu's insistence in 1977 that his origins were working class, Constantinescu told miners he was close to them as a geologist and knew the feeling of "getting out of the pit and seeing the sunshine".

He also said he was willing to forget the riots of the early 1990s, when thousands of Jiu Valley miners descended twice on Bucharest, beating up anti-communist student demonstrators and attacking public buildings.
"I know there was a time when we were on different sides of the barricades," he said. "Hate cannot be used as a building material. We need solidarity now to build a new Romania." 021424 GMT aug 97
